text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- German conservative Christian-Democrat Karl Lamers said at a meeting in Lower Austria this weekend that NATO should put greater focus on Europe so as to facilitate Austria's membership in the military alliance. Conservative People's Party wants the country's neutrality law to be amended to enable NATO entry.

- Financial expert Helmut Frisch says Austria's pension level must be reduced to secure the future of the pension system. He says structural measures in the government's planned reform of the public pensions are missing.
- Over 60 percent of Austrians say the current debate on political influence in the country's banks is harming Austria's industry. One in three Austrians believes this influence should be maintained.

- The practice of giving stock options to manangement employees is becoming increasingly popular among companies in Austria. Amendments to the laws should now improve the legal status of these options. High-grade steelmaker Boehler-Uddeholm will start a stock option programme next year.
- The energy agency says Austria's regional and federal grid operators should join together in a single network to secure their future ahead of the liberalisation of the electricity market.

- Post & Telekom Austria's financial chief Johannes Ditz says the company's privatisation is impossible without a social plan for its employees. However conservatives have recently criticised the negotiated plan to reduce the workforce by supporting early retirement.

- Upper Austria economic official Christoph Leitl welcomes the plan of federal grid company Verbund and regional energy providers EVN and Wiener Stadtwerke to join together in a bid to take over the state's 25-percent stake in its energy provider OKA.
- The number of exporters is expected to rise to 20,000 from 12,000 within five years, with the government's planned export offensive to start in 1998.

- The conservative People's Party wants to replace compulsory military service and the social service by a six-month "solidarity service". The party's chief whip Andreas Khol says Austria must take part in NATO's first expansion round in 1999. The country's army should be transformed into a professional task force including a militia.
